Vignette: Harjinder

Harjinder is a 79-year-old South Asian man who has spent the better part of five decades trying to outrun a war that ended long before most of his coworkers were born. He came to this country as a young soldier's ghost — a man who had survived the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War but was never quite sure the surviving had been worth it. He settled, married, had children, divorced, and somewhere in all of that, kept working. He still works. Five days a week, he moves through the aisles of a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city, checking inventory, lifting when his back allows, existing in the low hum of fluorescent lights and the beep of forklifts. His supervisors describe him as reliable and quiet. He would say the same of himself.

What happened to Harjinder happened in a rice field near a village whose name he still cannot say aloud. He was twenty-six years old. His unit was ambushed. He watched the man beside him — a friend since childhood, someone whose mother made him tea — take a burst of fire to the chest and fall without a sound. Harjinder ran. He has never forgiven himself for running, though he knows, intellectually, that running is why he is alive. He carried two other wounded men to cover that day. He received a commendation. He has never once looked at it.

For years, the memories stayed manageable — surfacing mostly at night, dissolving by morning. He married in his late twenties, had three children, and built a life that looked, from the outside, like recovery. But his wife eventually told him she felt she was living with a man who was always somewhere else. She was not wrong. The divorce, finalized when he was in his early fifties, left him in a small apartment with a television he rarely watches and a kitchen where he eats standing up.

Now the memories do not wait for night. The warehouse, ordinarily a comfort in its predictability, has become a minefield of triggers. Last month, a forklift backfired in the loading bay, and Harjinder dropped behind a pallet of boxed goods and stayed there, heart slamming, certain — for a full thirty seconds — that he was back in that field. A younger coworker found him and helped him up without comment. Harjinder thanked him and went to the bathroom and sat on a closed toilet lid until his hands stopped shaking. He told no one else.

He sleeps in fragments. Most nights he wakes between two and three in the morning with the specific, suffocating weight of the dream — always the same field, always the same friend falling — and then lies rigid until dawn, afraid to close his eyes again. He has developed a habit of leaving every light in his apartment on. His electricity bill is, he jokes without smiling, his most consistent expense.

He is irritable in ways that shame him. He snapped at his daughter during her last visit and watched her face close like a door. He has not called her back. He avoids crowded places — the temple he attended for thirty years, the Saturday market where he used to buy vegetables — because the noise and the press of bodies make him feel cornered and raw. He describes himself as "not a social man," but there is grief in the way he says it, as though he is mourning someone he used to be.

What strikes Harjinder most, sitting across from his therapist, is not the fear or even the exhaustion. It is the arithmetic of it — that he has been carrying this for fifty-three years, that the war was brief and his life has been long, and that somehow the brief thing has weighed more than all the rest of it combined. He picks at the hem of his jacket sleeve when he talks about this. He does not cry. He says he stopped being able to cry sometime in the 1980s, and he is not sure whether that is a loss or a mercy.
